newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Australia PM's Indonesia trip focuses on economics.
newsitem.headline: Australia PM's Indonesia trip focuses on economics.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Tuesday he had chosen to focus on economic matters rather than Indonesian domestic political issues on his first official visit to Jakarta.
"Most of our discussions today were about what we could do to deepen the economic relationship," Howard said after a 90-minute meeting with Indonesian President Suharto.
"I made a deliberate decision in coming here not to get involved in the domestic political debate in Indonesia," he said.

Howard said the leaders did not discuss riots in Jakarta in July, in which at least five people died. The riots, the worst in the city in more than 20 years, were sparked by a police raid on the headquarters of the minority Indonesian Democratic Party.

But Howard told a news conference that he had raised the issue of human rights in general and specifically the former Portuguese colony of East Timor with Suharto in their meeting at Jakarta's Freedom Palace.
The conservative leader arrived on Monday for his first official visit to Indonesia since taking office six months ago. He was due to leave for Japan on Wednesday.
"It is important to Australia that this be a visit which allows both President Suharto and myself to affirm the importance of the relationship," Howard said.
"It is a relationship that will never be based on uncritical acceptance of everything that occurs in the other country and that applies on both sides," he said.

"But it has survived and shown great durability because of the determination on the part of successive leaders in Australia and one leader since 1968 to place the broader interests above personal unhappiness with domestic occurences," he added.
Howard had been due to visit Indonesia in mid-August, but the trip was postponed because of his wife's illness.

"Both leaders agreed there was a need for exchanges and visits between officials, private businessmen and other members of society. Both leaders also mentioned the importance of media relations," Indonesian State Secretary Murdiono told reporters after the meeting.
He said the two leaders discussed their respective positions ahead of the November meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Manila.
"Both leaders hoped the APEC action plan of the each country could be made more concrete," Murdiono said.

Howard said Indonesia and Australia had a similar perspective on the admission of new members to the 18-member grouping with both agreeing to "hasten slowly" and achieve consensus before allowing new countries to join.
Suharto had also asked Australia to consider buying aircraft from its state-owned plane maker, Murdiono said.
The Australian leader later told a business lunch that the two countries' economies were complementary in many respects.

"The statistics bear this out. Australian exports to Indonesia grew by over 30 percent in 1995-96. Indonesia's exports to Australia grew by 27 percent in the same year and have doubled since 1991," Howard said.
"Australia now has 300 companies operating in Indonesia. The Indonesian government approved about A$4.5 billion in new investment proposals by Australian companies in 1995," he said.
Indonesia is Australia's fastest-growing market, and two-way trade in 1995-96 was worth A$4.2 billion ($3.3 billion).
